stem: A 59-year-old man undergoes excision of a benign parotid tumor. Postoperatively, he cannot elevate the right corner of his mouth when smiling or compress his right cheek against his teeth. However, he retains normal sensation over the cheek and normal masseter strength. Which structure was most likely injured?
options: Mandibular division of CN V
Buccal branches of CN VII
Buccal sensory nerve of CN V3
Auriculotemporal nerve
Glossopharyngeal nerve
explanation: Buccal branches of CN VII control muscles including buccinator and other facial expression muscles. Mastication and facial sensation are mediated by CN V.

stem: A patient develops reduced saliva production from the left parotid gland following surgery in the infratemporal fossa. Facial expression and mastication remain intact. The surgeon suspects interruption of postganglionic parasympathetic fibers immediately distal to their synapse. Which nerve normally carries these fibers to the parotid gland?
options: Greater petrosal nerve
Chorda tympani
Auriculotemporal nerve
Buccal branch of facial nerve
Lesser occipital nerve
explanation: CN IX secretomotor fibers synapse in the otic ganglion, then travel with the auriculotemporal nerve (V3) to the parotid.

stem: Following a mandibular fracture, a patient experiences difficulty protruding the jaw. During attempted opening, the mandible deviates to the left. There is no weakness of facial expression. Which combination most accurately identifies the impaired muscle and its nerve?
options: Left medial pterygoid — CN VII
Right masseter — CN V2
Left lateral pterygoid — CN V3
Right temporalis — CN VII
Left buccinator — CN V3
explanation: Weakness of the left lateral pterygoid causes the jaw to deviate left because the intact right lateral pterygoid acts unopposed.

stem: A 24-year-old develops a severe infection along the lateral aspect of the nose. Several days later, he presents with fever, proptosis, ophthalmoplegia, and impaired abduction of one eye. Imaging demonstrates cavernous sinus thrombosis. Which venous pathway most directly explains the intracranial spread of infection?
options: Facial vein → retromandibular vein → external jugular vein
Facial vein → angular vein → superior ophthalmic vein → cavernous sinus
Facial vein → superficial temporal vein → transverse sinus
Facial vein → maxillary vein → straight sinus
Facial vein → anterior jugular vein → inferior petrosal sinus
explanation: Facial venous drainage communicates with the cavernous sinus through the angular and superior ophthalmic veins.

stem: A newborn has a unilateral cleft extending from the upper lip toward the nostril, without involvement of the posterior secondary palate. The defect reflects failure of fusion between two facial prominences. Which structures failed to unite?
options: Lateral nasal and mandibular prominences
Medial nasal and maxillary prominences
Left and right mandibular prominences
Maxillary and lateral nasal prominences
Left and right palatine shelves
explanation: Cleft lip arises when the maxillary prominence fails to fuse with the medial nasal prominence.

stem: A newborn has an isolated cleft involving the posterior hard palate and soft palate, while the lip and primary palate are intact. Failure of which embryological event most directly accounts for this defect?
options: Fusion of the medial nasal prominences
Formation of the frontonasal prominence
Fusion of the lateral palatine shelves
Formation of Meckel cartilage
Fusion of the mandibular prominences
explanation: The secondary palate forms through elevation and fusion of the lateral palatine shelves.

stem: An infant has hypocalcemic seizures, recurrent infections, low circulating T cells, and an interrupted aortic arch. Genetic analysis demonstrates a chromosome 22q11.2 deletion. Disruption of neural crest contributions to which pharyngeal structures most directly explains the endocrine and immune abnormalities?
options: First and second arches
First and second clefts
Second and third clefts
Third and fourth pouches
Fourth and sixth arches only
explanation: DiGeorge syndrome disrupts development of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches, affecting thymus and parathyroid development.

stem: A child is evaluated for severe mandibular hypoplasia, malar hypoplasia, downward-slanting palpebral fissures, and abnormal external ears. Cardiac and thymic development are normal. Which embryologic mechanism best explains the craniofacial abnormalities?
options: Failure of forebrain separation
Abnormal migration or survival of neural crest cells contributing to the first pharyngeal arch
Failure of fusion between the lateral palatine shelves
Failed development of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches
Failed caudal neuropore closure
explanation: Treacher Collins syndrome involves abnormal first-arch neural crest development, producing characteristic mandibular and zygomatic abnormalities.

stem: A patient undergoes thyroidectomy and subsequently has a weak, breathy voice. Laryngoscopy reveals that the right vocal fold cannot abduct normally. The patient can still produce some high-pitched sounds. Which structure was most likely injured?
options: Right external branch of superior laryngeal nerve
Right recurrent laryngeal nerve
Left hypoglossal nerve
Right glossopharyngeal nerve
Right internal branch of superior laryngeal nerve
explanation: The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies nearly all intrinsic laryngeal muscles, including the posterior cricoarytenoid, the primary vocal fold abductor.

stem: A patient undergoes lymph node biopsy in the right posterior triangle of the neck. Postoperatively, the patient develops right shoulder droop and difficulty elevating the shoulder against resistance. Turning the head to the left against resistance is also weakened. Which nerve was most likely injured?
options: Right hypoglossal nerve
Right phrenic nerve
Right spinal accessory nerve
Right vagus nerve
Right dorsal scapular nerve
explanation: CN XI innervates ipsilateral trapezius and sternocleidomastoid. The right SCM rotates the head toward the left.

stem: Following a penetrating injury to the upper neck, a patient develops right-sided ptosis, miosis, and diminished facial sweating. Pupillary constriction in response to light remains intact. The injury most likely disrupted which structure?
options: Right cervical sympathetic chain
Right oculomotor nerve
Right optic nerve
Right facial nerve
Right ciliary ganglion
explanation: Cervical sympathetic injury produces ipsilateral Horner syndrome: miosis, mild ptosis, and potentially anhidrosis.

stem: A 41-year-old reports vertical diplopia that becomes particularly troublesome when walking downstairs or reading. The symptoms improve when the patient tilts the head away from the affected eye. Which pairing correctly identifies the dysfunctional muscle and the cranial nerve’s distinctive brainstem exit?
options: Inferior rectus — ventral midbrain
Superior oblique — dorsal midbrain
Lateral rectus — pontomedullary junction
Inferior oblique — dorsal pons
Superior rectus — ventral medulla
explanation: CN IV innervates superior oblique and uniquely exits dorsally from the brainstem. Weakness causes vertical diplopia, especially with downgaze.

stem: A patient develops sudden left ptosis, a dilated nonreactive left pupil, and a left eye positioned down and outward. CT angiography reveals a vascular lesion adjacent to the posterior communicating artery. Which finding best distinguishes the suspected compressive neuropathy from a typical microvascular ischemic neuropathy of the same cranial nerve?
options: Inability to abduct the eye
Loss of corneal sensation
Pupillary dilation due to involvement of superficial parasympathetic fibers
Ipsilateral facial paralysis
Loss of the afferent pupillary light reflex
explanation: Compressive CN III lesions commonly involve superficial parasympathetic fibers, producing mydriasis. Microvascular lesions often spare the pupil.

stem: An enlarging skull-base mass compresses the jugular foramen. The patient develops dysphagia, loss of the gag reflex, hoarseness, and ipsilateral shoulder weakness. Which additional finding would most strongly suggest that the lesion has extended beyond the jugular foramen to involve the hypoglossal canal?
options: Ipsilateral loss of hearing
Ipsilateral tongue deviation on protrusion
Contralateral loss of facial pain
Ipsilateral facial paralysis
Impaired abduction of the ipsilateral eye
explanation: CN XII traverses the hypoglossal canal, not the jugular foramen. A unilateral peripheral XII lesion makes the protruded tongue deviate toward the injury.

stem: A patient develops a facial nerve lesion in the facial canal proximal to the origins of the greater petrosal nerve, nerve to stapedius, and chorda tympani. Which combination of findings is most consistent with the lesion?
options: Facial paralysis, hyperacusis, loss of anterior two-thirds tongue taste, and reduced lacrimation
Facial paralysis with preserved taste, normal lacrimation, and normal hearing sensitivity
Loss of facial sensation, impaired mastication, and loss of parotid secretion
Facial paralysis, loss of posterior one-third tongue taste, and impaired swallowing
Loss of lacrimation with preserved facial expression and preserved taste
explanation: A proximal CN VII lesion affects facial expression, lacrimation, stapedius, and chorda tympani functions.

stem: A patient with a lesion of the left cavernous sinus cannot abduct the left eye. All other extraocular movements remain intact, and there is no ptosis or pupillary abnormality. Which nerve and muscle are affected?
options: CN III — medial rectus
CN IV — superior oblique
CN VI — lateral rectus
CN III — inferior oblique
CN V1 — superior rectus
explanation: CN VI supplies lateral rectus, which abducts the eye. An isolated lesion prevents ipsilateral abduction.

stem: A newborn with a lumbosacral myelomeningocele develops hydrocephalus. MRI demonstrates inferior displacement of the cerebellar vermis and brainstem through the foramen magnum. Which congenital abnormality best explains the constellation of findings?
options: Chiari I malformation
Chiari II malformation
Dandy–Walker malformation
Holoprosencephaly
Lissencephaly
explanation: Chiari II is strongly associated with lumbosacral myelomeningocele, hindbrain displacement, and hydrocephalus.

stem: A developmental mutation selectively disrupts sonic hedgehog signaling from the notochord and floor plate during neural tube regionalization. Which abnormality would most directly result?
options: Failed induction of dorsal sensory interneuron populations by BMP
Abnormal specification of ventral motor neuron populations
Failure of neural crest formation exclusively in cranial placodes
Failure of cerebral cortical neurons to migrate inside-out
Isolated agenesis of the choroid plexus
explanation: Sonic hedgehog from the notochord and floor plate promotes ventral neural tube differentiation, including motor neuron development.

stem: A brain biopsy demonstrates a cortical structure containing a superficial molecular layer, a single prominent row of large flask-shaped neurons, and a deep densely packed granular layer. Which cell type is primarily responsible for inhibitory output from this cortical structure to deep nuclei?
options: Pyramidal neurons
Purkinje cells
Granule cells
Oligodendrocytes
Ependymal cells
explanation: Purkinje neurons form a single cortical layer and provide GABAergic inhibitory output to deep cerebellar nuclei.

stem: A peripheral nerve biopsy demonstrates destruction of the connective tissue layer surrounding individual nerve fascicles, while the connective tissue around the entire nerve remains intact. Which structure has been selectively damaged?
options: Endoneurium
Epineurium
Perineurium
Neurilemma
Pia mater
explanation: Perineurium surrounds nerve fascicles; endoneurium surrounds individual fibers, and epineurium surrounds the overall nerve.

stem: A neuropathologist applies a Nissl stain to a region of cerebral cortex. Large neuronal somata are strongly stained, while myelinated axonal tracts are relatively poorly highlighted. Which cellular structure accounts for the prominent staining within neuronal cell bodies?
options: Smooth endoplasmic reticulum
Rough endoplasmic reticulum and associated ribosomes
Mitochondrial inner membranes
Microtubule-associated myelin proteins
Synaptic vesicle membranes
explanation: Nissl substance consists predominantly of rough ER and ribosomes, reflecting high neuronal protein synthesis.

stem: A demyelinating disease selectively destroys cells that produce multiple myelin internodes along different axons in the CNS. Which characteristic distinguishes the affected cells from their peripheral counterparts?
options: They originate from the endoneurium
They produce myelin around a single segment of one axon exclusively
They can myelinate segments of multiple different axons
They form the blood–CSF barrier in the ventricles
They are the principal phagocytes of the nervous system
explanation: One CNS oligodendrocyte can myelinate multiple axons; a myelinating Schwann cell typically forms one internode on one axon.

stem: A neurotoxin selectively inhibits cytoplasmic dynein-dependent axonal transport. A neuron exposed at its distal axon terminal subsequently fails to transport signaling endosomes and certain internalized toxins toward its soma. Which transport process has been impaired?
options: Fast anterograde transport toward the synaptic terminal
Retrograde microtubule-based transport toward the cell body
Actin-dependent vesicle transport across the synaptic cleft
Movement of electrical impulses by saltatory conduction
Passive diffusion of neurotransmitters along the axon
explanation: Dynein mediates retrograde microtubule transport toward the soma; kinesin primarily mediates anterograde transport.

stem: A histological section displays six layers of neuronal organization, including a prominent internal granular layer receiving thalamocortical inputs and an internal pyramidal layer containing major cortical projection neurons. Which tissue is being examined?
options: Cerebellar cortex
Cerebral neocortex
Spinal cord gray matter
Dorsal root ganglion
Superior cervical ganglion
explanation: Cerebral neocortex has six layers; the cerebellar cortex has three principal layers.

stem: A 27-year-old with suspected demyelinating disease undergoes MRI. The radiologist seeks a sequence that suppresses free CSF signal while retaining T2 sensitivity to periventricular white matter abnormalities. Which MRI sequence is most appropriate?
options: T1-weighted without contrast
T2-weighted without fluid suppression
FLAIR
Susceptibility-weighted imaging
Time-of-flight MR angiography
explanation: FLAIR suppresses free-fluid CSF signal, improving visualization of T2-hyperintense lesions near ventricles.

stem: A 28-year-old woman with obesity develops daily headaches, pulsatile tinnitus, transient visual obscurations, and horizontal diplopia. Fundoscopy reveals bilateral papilledema. MRI excludes an intracranial mass and venous sinus thrombosis. Lumbar puncture demonstrates elevated opening pressure and normal CSF composition. Which treatment most directly addresses the proposed pathophysiological mechanism?
options: Acetazolamide to reduce CSF production
High-dose levodopa to improve cerebral perfusion
Nimodipine to prevent vasospasm
Mannitol as indefinite outpatient maintenance therapy
Carbamazepine to suppress trigeminal activity
explanation: Acetazolamide inhibits carbonic anhydrase, reducing CSF production. Weight management is another important IIH treatment.

stem: A 67-year-old arrives 35 minutes after developing sudden aphasia and right hemiplegia. Emergency imaging must rapidly exclude intracranial hemorrhage before considering reperfusion treatment. Which imaging study should generally be obtained first?
options: MRI with gadolinium enhancement
Noncontrast head CT
MR spectroscopy
PET scan
T1-weighted MRI without contrast
explanation: Noncontrast CT rapidly identifies intracranial hemorrhage during acute stroke assessment.

stem: A 19-year-old cyclist strikes the temporal region of his head. He briefly loses consciousness, becomes lucid, and then develops rapid neurological deterioration. Head CT reveals a biconvex extra-axial hematoma that does not cross cranial sutures. Which vascular structure is most likely torn?
options: Bridging veins
Middle meningeal artery
Superior sagittal sinus
Middle cerebral artery
Anterior communicating artery
explanation: Middle meningeal artery injury near the pterion commonly produces a biconvex epidural hematoma.

stem: An 82-year-old patient taking anticoagulation develops worsening confusion several weeks after a minor fall. CT reveals a crescent-shaped extra-axial collection that extends across cranial sutures but is limited by dural reflections. The most likely disrupted structures traverse which anatomical space?
options: Between the calvarium and periosteal dura
Between meningeal dura and arachnoid mater
Between arachnoid mater and pia mater
Between pia mater and cerebral cortex
Between ependyma and choroid plexus
explanation: Subdural hematomas usually follow rupture of bridging veins and accumulate between dura and arachnoid.

stem: A child presents with worsening headaches and vomiting. MRI demonstrates markedly enlarged lateral and third ventricles, with a normal-sized fourth ventricle. Obstruction at which site best accounts for the imaging pattern?
options: Foramen of Magendie
Arachnoid granulations
Cerebral aqueduct
Central canal of the spinal cord
Paired lateral apertures of the fourth ventricle
explanation: Aqueductal obstruction enlarges the lateral and third ventricles while leaving the fourth ventricle relatively normal.

stem: A patient develops a rapidly expanding right temporal intracranial mass. Neurologic examination reveals a dilated, poorly reactive right pupil and progressive left-sided weakness. Imaging demonstrates displacement of the medial temporal lobe across the tentorial notch. Which structure is being directly compressed to explain the pupillary abnormality?
options: Right optic nerve
Right oculomotor nerve
Left trochlear nerve
Right abducens nerve
Right sympathetic chain
explanation: Uncal herniation can compress ipsilateral CN III, causing a dilated pupil and impaired pupillary light response.

stem: Two patients sustain complete axonal injuries. One has transection of a peripheral nerve, while the other has traumatic interruption of an axon within the CNS. Both develop Wallerian degeneration distal to the injury. Which mechanism best explains why meaningful axonal regeneration is more likely in the first patient?
options: CNS oligodendrocytes actively stimulate growth-cone formation
Peripheral macrophages prevent Schwann-cell proliferation
Schwann cells form regeneration-supporting pathways, while CNS myelin-associated inhibitors and glial scarring restrict growth
CNS neurons lack the ability to synthesize cytoskeletal proteins
Wallerian degeneration occurs only in peripheral nerves
explanation: PNS Schwann cells facilitate regeneration; the CNS environment contains inhibitory myelin molecules and glial scarring.

stem: A 63-year-old develops rapidly progressive bilateral leg weakness, saddle anesthesia, and urinary dysfunction. Examination reveals relatively symmetric perineal sensory loss, early loss of sphincter control, and mixed upper and lower motor neuron findings in the lower extremities. Radicular pain is minimal. Which diagnosis best explains the presentation?
options: Left L5 radiculopathy
Cauda equina syndrome
Conus medullaris syndrome
Brown–Séquard syndrome
Isolated pudendal neuropathy
explanation: Conus medullaris syndrome often produces early sphincter dysfunction, relatively symmetric saddle deficits, and mixed UMN/LMN findings.

stem: A small infarction selectively damages the left medullary pyramid immediately rostral to the pyramidal decussation. The corticospinal tracts in the spinal cord remain intact. Which motor findings would be expected after the acute period?
options: Left-sided spastic weakness and hyperreflexia
Right-sided spastic weakness and hyperreflexia
Left-sided flaccid paralysis with permanent areflexia and marked early atrophy
Bilateral symmetric lower motor neuron weakness
Right-sided loss of pain and temperature without weakness
explanation: A lesion above the pyramidal decussation produces contralateral UMN weakness. Left medullary pyramid damage affects right-sided movement.

stem: A patient with severe traumatic brain injury demonstrates extension of both upper and lower extremities in response to painful stimulation. Imaging shows damage to the upper brainstem that functionally eliminates descending influences from the red nucleus while leaving powerful vestibulospinal extensor drive intact. Which mechanism most directly accounts for the posture?
options: Isolated corticospinal interruption above the red nucleus with preserved rubrospinal facilitation of upper-extremity flexors
Bilateral injury to peripheral motor neurons
Loss of rubrospinal flexor influence with relatively unopposed vestibulospinal and pontine reticulospinal extensor activity
Increased activity of the dorsal column–medial lemniscus pathway
Selective interruption of the spinothalamic tract
explanation: Extensor posturing reflects loss of rubrospinal flexor influence with relatively unopposed extensor-promoting descending pathways.

stem: Touching the left cornea produces no blink in either eye. Touching the right cornea causes both eyes to blink normally. Voluntary bilateral eye closure remains intact. Which lesion best explains the findings?
options: Left facial nerve lesion
Right facial nerve lesion
Left ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve lesion
Right ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve lesion
Bilateral facial nerve lesions
explanation: Left V1 supplies the corneal afferent limb. Intact bilateral blinking after touching the right cornea demonstrates preserved CN VII efferents.

stem: A 29-year-old experiences a shimmering zigzag pattern in the right visual field that gradually expands over 20 minutes, followed by a unilateral throbbing headache, nausea, and photophobia. The patient has had four similar episodes. Neurological examination is normal between attacks. Which feature most strongly favors migraine aura over a transient ischemic attack?
options: Visual symptoms involving one hemifield
Recurrent transient neurological symptoms
Gradual progression of positive visual phenomena over several minutes
Complete resolution of visual symptoms
Headache occurring after the neurologic symptoms
explanation: Gradually spreading positive visual phenomena are characteristic of migraine aura. TIAs more often produce sudden-onset negative deficits.

stem: A 37-year-old man reports excruciating unilateral orbital pain lasting approximately 45 minutes. Episodes occur nightly for several weeks and are associated with ipsilateral lacrimation, nasal congestion, and mild ptosis. During attacks, he paces continuously. Which acute treatment combination is most appropriate?
options: Oral acetaminophen and amitriptyline
High-flow oxygen and subcutaneous sumatriptan
Carbamazepine and gabapentin
Propranolol and topiramate
Acetazolamide and corticosteroid taper
explanation: Acute cluster headache treatment includes high-flow oxygen and rapidly administered triptans, particularly subcutaneous sumatriptan.

stem: A 73-year-old develops a new temporal headache, scalp tenderness, fatigue, and jaw pain while chewing. ESR and CRP are elevated. During the interview, the patient describes a brief episode of painless monocular vision loss. Which is the most appropriate immediate management?
options: Reassure and observe because the visual symptoms resolved
Begin migraine prophylaxis and arrange outpatient MRI
Start high-dose glucocorticoids immediately while arranging confirmatory evaluation for giant cell arteritis
Perform lumbar puncture to assess CSF opening pressure before treatment
Begin triptan treatment and reassess in one week
explanation: Suspected giant cell arteritis with visual symptoms requires immediate glucocorticoids to reduce the risk of permanent vision loss.

stem: A 52-year-old develops an explosive headache that reaches maximum intensity within seconds. The patient vomits and briefly loses consciousness. Examination reveals neck stiffness but no focal motor deficit. Which diagnostic study is the most appropriate initial investigation?
options: EEG
Noncontrast CT of the head
Cervical spine radiographs
MRI of the pituitary gland
Electromyography
explanation: A thunderclap headache raises concern for subarachnoid hemorrhage; noncontrast CT is the initial investigation.

stem: A 26-year-old woman presents with new horizontal diplopia and an internuclear ophthalmoplegia. She recalls a painful episode of monocular visual loss eight months earlier that resolved without treatment. MRI demonstrates periventricular and juxtacortical lesions, including both gadolinium-enhancing and nonenhancing plaques. Which interpretation is most accurate?
options: The findings demonstrate an isolated peripheral demyelinating disorder
The lesions suggest dissemination in space and time, supporting multiple sclerosis
The findings establish acute disseminated encephalomyelitis because more than one lesion is present
The absence of spinal cord symptoms excludes multiple sclerosis
The lesions indicate osmotic demyelination of the central pons
explanation: Separate clinical attacks and MRI lesions in characteristic regions, with different enhancement states, support dissemination in time and space.

stem: A 9-year-old child develops fever, headache, confusion, ataxia, and multifocal neurological deficits approximately two weeks after a viral infection. MRI reveals large, poorly demarcated, multifocal white matter lesions. There is no previous history of neurological attacks. Which diagnosis is most likely?
options: Relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis
Charcot–Marie–Tooth disease
Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
Central pontine myelinolysis
explanation: ADEM typically presents as a monophasic postinfectious inflammatory demyelinating syndrome with encephalopathy, particularly in children.

stem: A patient sustains a selective lesion of the right anterolateral funiculus at the T7 spinal cord level. The dorsal columns and motor pathways remain intact. Which sensory deficit is most likely?
options: Loss of right-sided vibration and position sensation below T7
Loss of left-sided pain and temperature beginning approximately one to two spinal levels below the lesion
Loss of right-sided pain and temperature beginning at the midbrain
Bilateral loss of facial pain and temperature
Loss of left-sided discriminative touch with preserved pain sensation
explanation: Spinothalamic fibers cross within the spinal cord, generally after ascending roughly one to two segments, producing contralateral deficits below injury.

stem: A patient with a healed peripheral nerve injury experiences severe pain when lightly brushing the skin over the affected region. Repeated nociceptive input has produced increased excitability in dorsal horn neurons, including activity-dependent NMDA receptor signaling. Which combination best describes the clinical phenomenon and its underlying mechanism?
options: Hyperalgesia caused by complete loss of nociceptors
Allodynia associated with central sensitization
Analgesia caused by descending serotonergic inhibition
Referred pain caused exclusively by peripheral axonal regeneration
Hypoalgesia caused by increased inhibitory interneuron activity
explanation: Allodynia is pain from a normally nonpainful stimulus. Persistent nociceptive activity can cause NMDA-dependent central sensitization.

stem: A patient receives an opioid for acute postoperative pain. Activation of presynaptic μ-opioid receptors in the dorsal horn decreases neurotransmitter release from primary nociceptive afferents. Which intracellular mechanism is primarily responsible?
options: Gs activation, increased cAMP, and enhanced calcium influx
Gq activation and increased phospholipase C activity
Gi/o signaling with reduced presynaptic calcium entry and increased postsynaptic potassium conductance
Direct activation of voltage-gated sodium channels
Competitive antagonism of NMDA receptors
explanation: μ-Opioid receptors are Gi/o-coupled. They inhibit presynaptic calcium entry and facilitate postsynaptic potassium conductance.

stem: A 58-year-old with painful diabetic polyneuropathy is prescribed duloxetine. After several weeks, the patient reports reduced burning and electric-shock-like pain without evidence of peripheral nerve regeneration. Which mechanism most directly explains the analgesic effect?
options: Selective blockade of peripheral voltage-gated sodium channels
Increased serotonin and norepinephrine signaling, enhancing descending pain inhibition
Irreversible inhibition of cyclooxygenase-1
Direct activation of μ-opioid receptors
Blockade of acetylcholinesterase at the neuromuscular junction
explanation: Duloxetine inhibits serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake, enhancing descending inhibitory pain modulation.

stem: A 56-year-old develops progressive weakness of right ankle dorsiflexion followed several weeks later by painful weakness of left wrist extension. Sensory deficits are asymmetric and involve multiple separate peripheral nerve territories. Laboratory studies reveal systemic inflammation. Which underlying pathophysiology is most consistent with the pattern?
options: Distal symmetric length-dependent neuropathy caused by diabetes
Multifocal ischemic nerve injury due to vasculitis
Selective degeneration of corticospinal motor neurons
Isolated posterior column demyelination
Symmetric hereditary demyelination from childhood
explanation: Asymmetric, painful involvement of separate nerves suggests mononeuritis multiplex, commonly associated with vasculitic ischemia.

stem: A patient undergoing treatment for tuberculosis develops distal paresthesias and burning discomfort. Examination reveals reduced pinprick sensation in a stocking distribution. The patient is taking isoniazid. Which intervention most directly addresses a preventable mechanism of this drug-associated neuropathy?
options: Vitamin B1 supplementation
Vitamin B6 supplementation
Vitamin B12 restriction
Folate antagonism
Vitamin E restriction
explanation: Isoniazid can produce pyridoxine deficiency. Vitamin B6 supplementation helps prevent associated neuropathy.

stem: A patient develops rapidly ascending symmetric weakness and absent deep tendon reflexes ten days after a gastrointestinal infection. Nerve-conduction studies demonstrate slowed conduction and prolonged distal latencies. CSF reveals elevated protein with relatively few leukocytes. Which process most directly explains the neurological findings?
options: Autoimmune destruction of CNS oligodendrocytes
Immune-mediated segmental demyelination of peripheral nerves and nerve roots
Degeneration of anterior horn cells
Primary loss of acetylcholine receptors at neuromuscular junctions
Selective infarction of the anterior spinal artery
explanation: AIDP, the common demyelinating form of Guillain–Barré syndrome, produces peripheral nerve/root demyelination, areflexia, and albuminocytologic dissociation.

stem: A 16-year-old has slowly progressive distal weakness, foot deformities, reduced tendon reflexes, and a family history of similar symptoms. Peripheral nerve biopsy demonstrates concentric Schwann-cell proliferations around repeatedly demyelinated and remyelinated axons. Which finding is most characteristic of this process?
options: Lewy bodies
Neurofibrillary tangles
Onion bulb formations
Negri bodies
Spongiform vacuolation
explanation: Onion bulbs reflect repeated demyelination and remyelination with concentric Schwann-cell processes, seen in certain CMT subtypes.

stem: A 48-year-old develops lower back pain radiating along the lateral leg to the dorsum of the foot. Examination reveals weakness of ankle dorsiflexion and great toe extension. Ankle inversion is also weakened, making an isolated common fibular neuropathy less likely. Which localization is most consistent with the findings?
options: L3 nerve root
L4 nerve root
L5 nerve root
S1 nerve root
Femoral nerve
explanation: L5 radiculopathy affects dorsiflexion, toe extension, and potentially inversion. Inversion is often preserved in isolated common fibular neuropathy.

stem: An infarct selectively damages the right nucleus gracilis in the caudal medulla, before the second-order neurons cross the midline. The nucleus cuneatus and adjacent motor pathways remain intact. Which deficit should be expected?
options: Loss of left lower-extremity vibration and proprioception
Loss of right lower-extremity vibration and proprioception
Loss of left upper-extremity pain and temperature
Loss of right facial discriminative touch
Bilateral loss of fine touch affecting the entire body
explanation: Nucleus gracilis receives ipsilateral lower-body DCML information before internal arcuate fibers decussate.

stem: A small left thalamic infarct selectively damages the ventral posteromedial nucleus, while sparing the ventral posterolateral nucleus. Which deficit is most likely?
options: Right-sided loss of discriminative facial touch
Left-sided loss of vibration throughout the body
Right-sided loss of fine touch limited to the lower extremity
Bilateral loss of the corneal blink motor response
Left-sided paralysis of the muscles of mastication
explanation: VPM processes contralateral facial somatosensation; VPL primarily processes contralateral body somatosensation.

stem: An elderly patient develops abrupt bilateral leg weakness after prolonged systemic hypotension. Examination reveals bilateral loss of pain and temperature sensation below the lesion, preserved vibration and joint-position sensation, and bladder dysfunction. MRI demonstrates infarction involving the anterior two-thirds of the spinal cord. Which arterial territory is most likely affected?
options: Posterior spinal arteries
Anterior spinal artery
Middle cerebral artery
Posterior inferior cerebellar artery
Anterior inferior cerebellar artery
explanation: Anterior spinal artery infarction affects descending motor and anterolateral sensory pathways while often sparing the posterior columns.

stem: A medical student is preparing to perform a lumbar puncture in an adult patient. The needle is inserted at the L4–L5 interspace to minimize the risk of directly injuring the spinal cord. Which anatomical relationship makes this approach relatively safe?
options: The spinal cord normally terminates at S2
The dural sac terminates at L1
The conus medullaris usually ends near L1–L2, while the lumbar cistern continues inferiorly
The cauda equina is separated from the subarachnoid space by the pia mater
The epidural space contains no vascular structures below L2
explanation: The adult conus ends near L1–L2, while the CSF-containing lumbar cistern extends farther inferiorly.

stem: A transverse section of the spinal cord demonstrates prominent dorsal and ventral horns, a distinct lateral horn containing sympathetic preganglionic neurons, and dorsal columns divided into fasciculi gracilis and cuneatus. Which spinal cord level is most consistent with the section?
options: C2
T2
L4
S3
explanation: T2 has an intermediolateral sympathetic cell column and both gracile and cuneate fasciculi. T10 lacks the cuneate fasciculus.

stem: A 71-year-old with cervical spondylosis sustains a hyperextension injury after falling forward. Examination reveals severe weakness of both hands and arms, comparatively mild leg weakness, and variable sensory deficits. Which spinal cord syndrome best explains the disproportionate upper-extremity involvement?
options: Anterior cord syndrome
Posterior cord syndrome
Central cord syndrome
Brown–Séquard syndrome
Cauda equina syndrome
explanation: Central cord syndrome commonly causes greater arm than leg weakness, especially following cervical hyperextension injury.

stem: A 62-year-old develops progressive gait instability, bilateral loss of vibration and position sensation in the feet, spasticity, and hyperreflexia. Pain and temperature sensation remain relatively intact. Laboratory testing reveals vitamin B12 deficiency. Which combination of spinal cord pathways is most likely affected?
options: Spinothalamic tracts and anterior horn cells
Dorsal columns and lateral corticospinal tracts
Ventral roots and dorsal root ganglia exclusively
Anterior white commissure and spinocerebellar tracts exclusively
Medial longitudinal fasciculus and vestibulospinal tracts
explanation: Subacute combined degeneration affects posterior columns and lateral corticospinal pathways, causing proprioceptive loss and UMN findings.

stem: An experimental neuron is exposed to a substantial increase in extracellular potassium concentration. Initially, its resting membrane potential becomes less negative. With sustained severe depolarization, the neuron becomes less capable of generating normal action potentials despite being closer to threshold. Which mechanism best explains the reduced excitability?
options: Increased potassium efflux produces persistent hyperpolarization
Persistent depolarization increases the proportion of voltage-gated sodium channels in the inactivated state
Voltage-gated sodium channels open more rapidly with each stimulus
Chloride equilibrium potential becomes increasingly positive
Sodium–potassium ATPase directly closes all voltage-gated calcium channels
explanation: Severe sustained depolarization promotes sodium-channel inactivation, impairing action potential initiation despite a less-negative resting potential.

stem: A genetic mutation reduces the conductance of delayed rectifier voltage-gated potassium channels without changing the properties of sodium channels. Recordings demonstrate an altered action potential waveform. Which change is most likely?
options: A faster repolarization phase and increased afterhyperpolarization
Failure of the initial sodium-dependent depolarizing upstroke
Prolonged action potential duration due to slower repolarization
Complete elimination of the absolute refractory period
A permanent shift of the sodium equilibrium potential toward zero
explanation: Delayed rectifier potassium channels help repolarize the membrane. Reduced activity broadens and prolongs action potentials.

stem: A 47-year-old man with Down syndrome develops progressive episodic memory impairment and spatial disorientation. MRI demonstrates medial temporal atrophy. Neuropathology reveals extracellular amyloid deposits and intracellular tangles containing hyperphosphorylated tau. Which molecular mechanism contributes to the elevated risk of this disease in individuals with trisomy 21?
options: Reduced production of α-synuclein
Increased gene dosage of amyloid precursor protein
Loss of the frataxin gene
Expansion of CAG repeats in the huntingtin gene
Increased degradation of amyloid precursor protein by α-secretase exclusively
explanation: Chromosome 21 contains APP. Increased APP dosage contributes to amyloid pathology and early Alzheimer disease risk in Down syndrome.

stem: A 59-year-old previously reserved accountant develops progressive disinhibition, compulsive eating, socially inappropriate behavior, and diminished empathy. Episodic memory is relatively preserved early in the course. MRI reveals disproportionate frontal and anterior temporal atrophy. Which pathological finding is most compatible with the diagnosis?
options: Extracellular neuritic plaques as the exclusive lesion
Intraneuronal inclusions containing TDP-43 or abnormal tau
Widespread prion-associated spongiform change
Lewy bodies confined to the substantia nigra
Primary inflammatory demyelination of the optic nerves
explanation: Frontotemporal degeneration can involve abnormal tau or TDP-43 inclusions, with early behavioral and language dysfunction.

stem: A 74-year-old develops progressive cognitive impairment with marked day-to-day fluctuations in attention, recurrent detailed visual hallucinations, and spontaneous parkinsonian features. His spouse reports that he frequently acts out dreams during sleep. Which abnormal protein is most strongly associated with the underlying disorder?
options: β-Amyloid exclusively
TDP-43 exclusively
α-Synuclein
Mutant prion protein exclusively
Frataxin
explanation: Dementia with Lewy bodies involves α-synuclein aggregates and commonly produces hallucinations, fluctuating cognition, parkinsonism, and REM sleep behavior disorder.

stem: A 9-year-old has numerous daily episodes of behavioral arrest lasting approximately 10 seconds. Hyperventilation during EEG produces generalized 3-Hz spike-and-wave discharges. A drug is prescribed that selectively reduces the thalamic pacemaker current responsible for this seizure type. Which mechanism is most directly targeted?
options: Prolongation of the inactivated state of voltage-gated sodium channels
Blockade of T-type voltage-gated calcium channels
Inhibition of synaptic vesicle protein SV2A
Increased GABA-A channel opening frequency
Irreversible inhibition of GABA transaminase
explanation: Ethosuximide reduces T-type calcium currents important in thalamic oscillations underlying typical absence seizures.

stem: A patient with recurrent focal seizures is started on levetiracetam. The clinician explains that its mechanism differs from drugs primarily acting on sodium-channel inactivation, thalamic T-type calcium channels, and GABA-A receptor activity. Which action best explains the medication's antiseizure effect?
options: Inhibition of the vesicular protein SV2A, modulating neurotransmitter release
Direct opening of GABA-A chloride channels in the absence of GABA
Selective antagonism of postsynaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptors
Inactivation of the neuronal sodium–potassium ATPase
Irreversible inhibition of acetylcholinesterase
explanation: Levetiracetam binds synaptic vesicle protein SV2A, modulating neurotransmitter release.

stem: A research participant receives a medication that selectively blocks muscarinic acetylcholine receptors. Following administration, sweating is markedly reduced despite preservation of sympathetic preganglionic transmission. Which characteristic of sympathetic innervation explains this result?
options: All sympathetic postganglionic neurons release norepinephrine
Sympathetic innervation of eccrine sweat glands commonly uses acetylcholine acting on muscarinic receptors
Eccrine sweat glands receive exclusively somatic motor innervation
Sympathetic preganglionic neurons release norepinephrine onto nicotinic receptors
Muscarinic receptors are confined to parasympathetic ganglia
explanation: Eccrine sweat glands are a classic exception: their sympathetic postganglionic neurons commonly release acetylcholine onto muscarinic receptors.

stem: A 33-year-old with a chronic complete spinal cord injury at T4 suddenly develops a severe headache, profuse sweating and flushing above the level of injury, bradycardia, and blood pressure of 210/110 mmHg. Examination reveals a distended urinary bladder. Which pathophysiological mechanism best explains the presentation?
options: Loss of all sympathetic outflow below the lesion causing diffuse hypotension
Uncontrolled sympathetic reflex activity below the spinal lesion triggered by a visceral stimulus, with impaired descending inhibition
Selective injury to parasympathetic neurons in the sacral spinal cord
Bilateral failure of carotid body chemoreceptors
Excessive voluntary activation of somatic motor neurons
explanation: Autonomic dysreflexia follows loss of descending control over sympathetic spinal reflexes, commonly triggered by bladder distension above T6 injuries.

stem: A patient suffers a small lesion selectively affecting the suprachiasmatic nucleus. The patient subsequently develops disrupted sleep-wake timing, abnormal circadian hormone rhythms, and difficulty synchronizing physiological cycles with the day-night environment. Which input normally provides the principal external timing signal to this nucleus?
options: Fornix from the hippocampus
Stria terminalis from the amygdala
Retinohypothalamic tract from the retina
Mammillothalamic tract from the mammillary bodies
Corticospinal tract from the motor cortex
explanation: The retinohypothalamic tract supplies light-related timing information directly to the suprachiasmatic nucleus.

stem: A patient develops pituitary stalk injury. The resulting disruption reduces hypothalamic hormone delivery through the portal circulation and impairs axonal transport to the posterior pituitary. Which hormonal pattern is most consistent with the loss of normal hypothalamic regulation?
options: Increased ACTH, increased TSH, and increased ADH
Decreased prolactin with increased ADH
Increased prolactin with reduced secretion of several other anterior pituitary hormones and impaired ADH release
Increased LH and FSH with normal prolactin
Isolated prolactin suppression without changes in other pituitary hormones
explanation: Pituitary stalk injury disrupts hypothalamic portal signals and posterior pituitary axons. Loss of tonic dopamine inhibition can raise prolactin.

stem: A patient with bilateral damage to the amygdala can identify objects and accurately describe emotionally threatening photographs but displays markedly reduced fear responses and diminished autonomic reactivity to conditioned threats. Which function of the amygdala has been most directly disrupted?
options: Primary discriminative touch processing
Association of sensory stimuli with emotional significance and generation of affective-autonomic responses
Encoding of spinal stretch reflexes
Direct control of corticospinal motor neurons
Generation of visual information in the retina
explanation: The amygdala attaches emotional significance to stimuli and participates in conditioned fear and autonomic responses.

stem: A patient undergoes focal injury to the anterior cingulate cortex. Following the lesion, the patient can detect and localize painful stimulation but reports markedly reduced emotional distress associated with the sensation. Which interpretation best explains the dissociation?
options: The anterior cingulate cortex principally mediates discriminative localization of tactile stimuli
The spinothalamic tract has been completely severed
The affective-motivational dimension of pain has been selectively disrupted
Peripheral nociceptors have undergone Wallerian degeneration
The medial lemniscus is responsible for the emotional unpleasantness of pain
explanation: The anterior cingulate contributes to the affective-motivational dimension of pain, distinct from sensory localization.

stem: Following bilateral medial temporal lobe injury, a patient cannot form new declarative memories. However, repeated practice of a mirror-tracing task leads to progressively improved performance, even though the patient has no conscious recollection of previous sessions. Which explanation best accounts for this pattern?
options: Procedural learning requires an intact hippocampus, whereas declarative memory does not
Hippocampal injury disrupts explicit memory formation while allowing some implicit skill-learning circuits to remain functional
The lesion selectively destroyed the primary motor cortex
Short-term working memory is exclusively dependent on the cerebellar vermis
The patient has isolated retrograde amnesia
explanation: The hippocampus is crucial for establishing explicit declarative memories; procedural skill learning can remain intact through other circuits.

stem: A lesion damages the fornix bilaterally, interrupting a major output pathway of the hippocampal formation. The patient subsequently develops impaired episodic memory. Which target normally receives hippocampal output through this pathway as part of the classic limbic memory circuit?
options: Mammillary bodies
Substantia nigra pars compacta
Ventral posterolateral thalamus
Inferior olivary nucleus
Dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus
explanation: The fornix carries major hippocampal outputs to the mammillary bodies, participating in the limbic memory circuit.

stem: In a hippocampal slice preparation, electrical stimulation of CA3 pyramidal neurons produces excitatory responses in CA1 pyramidal neurons. Repeated high-frequency stimulation leads to persistent strengthening of these synapses. Which named pathway carries the CA3-to-CA1 projections?
options: Perforant pathway
Mossy fibers
Schaffer collaterals
Mammillothalamic tract
Stria terminalis
explanation: Schaffer collaterals project from CA3 to CA1. Mossy fibers project from dentate gyrus to CA3.

stem: A research team attempts to induce long-term potentiation in a hippocampal synapse. Glutamate release is normal, but a drug prevents the postsynaptic NMDA receptor from conducting calcium during coincident depolarization. Which consequence is most likely?
options: Enhanced induction of LTP through increased calcium-dependent kinase activity
Failure to initiate normal NMDA-dependent LTP despite preserved fast AMPA-mediated synaptic responses
Complete prevention of all presynaptic action potentials
Permanent opening of voltage-gated potassium channels
Enhanced acetylcholine release from motor neurons
explanation: NMDA-dependent calcium entry initiates signaling important for LTP; AMPA responses can remain despite NMDA blockade.

stem: In an experimental hippocampal circuit, prolonged low-frequency stimulation produces a lasting reduction in synaptic strength. The effect is associated with relatively modest postsynaptic calcium signaling, activation of phosphatases, and removal of AMPA receptors from the postsynaptic membrane. Which form of plasticity is being demonstrated?
options: Post-tetanic potentiation
Long-term potentiation
Long-term depression
Saltatory conduction
Axonal regeneration
explanation: LTD can involve modest calcium signals, phosphatase activation, and AMPA receptor internalization, weakening synaptic transmission.

stem: A brain specimen from a patient with resting tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia, and postural instability demonstrates loss of pigmented neurons in the substantia nigra. Microscopy reveals intracytoplasmic eosinophilic inclusions. Which protein constitutes the characteristic aggregate?
options: Hyperphosphorylated tau
α-Synuclein
β-Amyloid
Prion protein exclusively
Frataxin
explanation: Parkinson disease characteristically involves substantia nigra dopaminergic neuron loss and α-synuclein-containing Lewy bodies.

stem: Brain tissue from a patient with rapidly progressive dementia, myoclonus, and ataxia demonstrates widespread microscopic vacuoles within the neuropil, neuronal loss, and gliosis, with minimal inflammatory infiltration. Which disease mechanism best explains the pathology?
options: An autoimmune attack against oligodendrocyte myelin
Propagation of abnormally folded prion protein that induces misfolding of normally structured protein
Accumulation of TDP-43 in anterior horn cells exclusively
Loss of dopamine-producing neurons due to a toxin affecting vesicular monoamine transport
Excess deposition of extracellular immunoglobulin light chains
explanation: CJD arises through propagation of misfolded prion proteins and produces spongiform neuropathology.

stem: A 17-year-old develops progressive gait ataxia, impaired position and vibration sense, absent ankle reflexes, and bilateral extensor plantar responses. Examination also reveals scoliosis and cardiomyopathy. Genetic testing identifies an autosomal recessive repeat expansion. Which molecular abnormality is most likely?
options: CAG expansion causing polyglutamine accumulation in huntingtin
GAA expansion reducing expression of frataxin
Trinucleotide expansion increasing expression of amyloid precursor protein
Deletion of the PMP22 gene in all affected individuals
Mutation producing constitutively active α-synuclein receptors
explanation: Friedreich ataxia is typically caused by autosomal recessive GAA repeat expansion in FXN, reducing frataxin expression.

stem: A 31-year-old suddenly experiences an unpleasant burning smell, followed by behavioral arrest, repetitive lip-smacking, and impaired responsiveness for approximately 90 seconds. The patient is confused afterward and cannot recall the episode. Which classification is most appropriate?
options: Generalized absence seizure
Focal aware seizure without impaired awareness
Focal impaired awareness seizure
Generalized atonic seizure
Myoclonic seizure
explanation: The aura suggests focal onset, while automatisms, impaired responsiveness, and postictal confusion support a focal impaired awareness seizure.

stem: An 8-year-old is repeatedly observed to stop speaking for 8–12 seconds, stare blankly, and then resume the interrupted activity without confusion. Hyperventilation provokes an episode during EEG monitoring. Which EEG finding is most characteristic?
options: Focal temporal sharp waves followed by prolonged postictal slowing
Generalized 3-Hz spike-and-wave discharges
Burst suppression pattern
Continuous generalized epileptiform activity lasting over five minutes
Isolated occipital delta slowing without epileptiform activity
explanation: Typical absence seizures produce generalized 3-Hz spike-and-wave activity, brief impaired awareness, and minimal postictal confusion.

stem: An experimental drug selectively inhibits voltage-gated calcium channels at presynaptic terminals. Axonal action potentials arrive normally, and postsynaptic ligand-gated receptors remain functional, but evoked synaptic currents are dramatically reduced. Which event has been most directly disrupted?
options: Propagation of the presynaptic action potential
Calcium-dependent synaptic vesicle fusion and neurotransmitter exocytosis
Generation of the resting membrane potential by potassium leak channels
Retrograde axonal transport from the synaptic terminal
Transcription of postsynaptic receptor genes
explanation: Presynaptic calcium influx triggers the vesicle-fusion machinery. Blocking calcium entry reduces transmitter release without necessarily blocking axonal action potentials.

stem: A neuron receives simultaneous excitatory postsynaptic inputs from several different presynaptic neurons. Individually, none produces enough depolarization at the axon initial segment to reach threshold. Together, the inputs trigger an action potential. Which physiological principle best explains the response?
options: Temporal summation of action potentials in one axon
Spatial summation of graded excitatory postsynaptic potentials
Saltatory conduction across multiple synapses
Absolute refractory period summation
Retrograde transport of excitatory neurotransmitters
explanation: Inputs from multiple separate synapses combine through spatial summation. Temporal summation involves repeated inputs over time.

stem: A research inhibitor selectively blocks the rate-limiting enzyme responsible for converting tyrosine into L-DOPA. The intervention reduces synthesis of multiple catecholaminergic neurotransmitters. Which pairing correctly identifies the enzyme and the neurotransmitters most directly affected?
options: Tryptophan hydroxylase — serotonin and melatonin
Glutamate decarboxylase — GABA and glycine
Tyrosine hydroxylase — dopamine and norepinephrine
Choline acetyltransferase — acetylcholine and dopamine
Monoamine oxidase — increased dopamine and norepinephrine synthesis
explanation: Tyrosine hydroxylase catalyzes tyrosine-to-L-DOPA conversion, the rate-limiting step of catecholamine synthesis.

stem: A patient sustains a deep laceration through the cheek that damages a facial expression muscle. Following the injury, the patient repeatedly traps food between the cheek and molar teeth while chewing. Masseter strength, facial cutaneous sensation, and jaw movement are intact. Which muscle shown in the figure was most likely injured?
options: Risorius
Masseter
Orbicularis oris
Buccinator
Zygomaticus major
explanation: Buccinator presses the cheek against the teeth, keeping food positioned for chewing. It receives CN VII motor innervation.

stem: A fracture extends through the infraorbital margin and damages the nerve emerging through the infraorbital foramen shown in the skull. The patient develops sensory loss over the lower eyelid, upper lip, and adjacent cheek. Which nerve division contains the injured sensory fibers?
options: CN V2
CN V1
CN V3
CN VII
C2 spinal nerve
explanation: The infraorbital nerve is a V2 branch carrying sensation from the cheek, upper lip, lower eyelid, and lateral nose.

stem: During surgery, a surgeon must reconstruct the duct of the parotid gland. The anatomy shown in the figure is used to identify the duct's relationship to the muscles of the superficial and deep face. Which description correctly traces its route toward the oral cavity?
options: It passes deep to the medial pterygoid and enters beside the mandibular third molar
It pierces the masseter directly and enters the floor of the mouth
It travels through the stylomastoid foramen and opens beneath the tongue
It follows the external jugular vein and enters the oropharynx
It crosses the masseter, turns medially, pierces the buccinator, and opens opposite the maxillary second molar
explanation: The parotid duct crosses the masseter, pierces buccinator, and opens near the maxillary second molar.

stem: A skull fracture occurs at the pterion, as shown in the figure. An associated arterial injury results in an enlarging extra-axial hematoma. Before reaching the inner surface of the cranium, the injured artery most directly passes through which opening?
options: Foramen rotundum
Foramen ovale
Foramen spinosum
Jugular foramen
Carotid canal
explanation: The middle meningeal artery enters the cranial cavity through the foramen spinosum after branching from the maxillary artery.

stem: During neck dissection, the surgeon identifies a small infrahyoid muscle extending from the thyroid cartilage to the hyoid bone. Unlike most other infrahyoid muscles, it receives motor fibers from C1 traveling briefly with the hypoglossal nerve rather than primarily through the ansa cervicalis. Which muscle is being identified?
options: Thyrohyoid
Sternohyoid
Sternothyroid
Omohyoid
Mylohyoid
explanation: Thyrohyoid receives C1 motor fibers that travel with CN XII. Most other infrahyoid muscles receive ansa cervicalis branches.

stem: A patient has a left-hemispheric cortical infarction resulting in nonfluent, effortful speech with relatively preserved auditory comprehension. The patient recognizes the intended words but struggles to generate fluent spoken language. Which location is most consistent with the lesion?
options: Right superior temporal gyrus
Left primary visual cortex
Left postcentral gyrus
Left inferior frontal gyrus
Right occipital association cortex
explanation: Broca's area in the dominant inferior frontal gyrus supports fluent motor-language production.

stem: An infarction involving the medial surface of the left frontal lobe selectively damages the lower-extremity representation of the primary motor cortex. The lateral convexity of the precentral gyrus is spared. Which finding would be expected?
options: Predominantly left-sided arm weakness
Right-sided visual field loss
Bilateral paralysis of facial expression
Isolated loss of right facial fine touch
Predominantly right-sided leg weakness
explanation: The primary motor representation of the lower extremity lies medially, largely in the paracentral lobule, and controls the contralateral leg.

stem: A destructive lesion involves the paired rounded structures visible on the inferior aspect of the brain posterior to the infundibulum. These structures participate in a limbic circuit important for memory. Which structures have most likely been damaged?
options: Inferior colliculi
Optic tracts
Mammillary bodies
Cerebral peduncles
Olfactory bulbs
explanation: Mammillary bodies lie posterior to the infundibulum and participate in memory circuitry.

stem: A focal lesion damages the paired elevations on the dorsal midbrain that participate in orienting eye movements toward visual stimuli. The adjacent paired elevations primarily involved in auditory processing remain intact. Which structures are damaged?
options: Superior colliculi
Inferior colliculi
Mammillary bodies
Gracile tubercles
Olivary nuclei
explanation: Superior colliculi coordinate visually guided orienting responses; inferior colliculi participate primarily in auditory processing.

stem: In the coronal brain section shown, a prominent gray matter nucleus forms part of the lateral wall of the anterior horn of the lateral ventricle. It lies medial to the anterior limb of the internal capsule. Which structure is being described?
options: Putamen
Head of the caudate nucleus
Globus pallidus
Claustrum
Amygdala
explanation: The head of the caudate lies beside the anterior horn of the lateral ventricle, medial to the anterior limb of the internal capsule.

stem: The section demonstrates deep nuclei and adjacent white matter. A small left-sided infarct selectively damages the compact descending motor fibers located between the thalamus medially and the lentiform nucleus laterally. Which structure is the most likely site of injury?
options: Anterior commissure
External capsule
Corpus callosum
Cingulum
Posterior limb of the internal capsule
explanation: The posterior limb of the internal capsule lies between thalamus and lentiform nucleus and carries concentrated motor fibers.

stem: The figure displays the hippocampal formation and its associated white matter. A thin collection of fibers runs along the hippocampal surface and gathers into a larger tract that eventually forms the crus of the fornix. Which structure is being identified at the hippocampal surface?
options: Internal capsule
Stria terminalis
Mammillothalamic tract
Fimbria of the hippocampus
Medial lemniscus
explanation: The fimbria collects hippocampal efferent fibers and continues posteriorly into the fornix.

stem: The dissected dorsal diencephalon demonstrates a small midline structure near the posterior roof of the third ventricle, immediately superior to the superior colliculi. This structure participates in circadian endocrine signaling. Which structure is being described?
options: Habenular nucleus
Pineal gland
Anterior thalamic nucleus
Mammillary body
Subthalamic nucleus
explanation: The pineal gland lies near the posterior roof of the third ventricle and produces melatonin for circadian signaling.

stem: A patient develops an isolated lesion of the left cerebellar hemisphere. Motor strength is preserved, but the patient demonstrates dysmetria during finger-to-nose testing, intention tremor, and impaired coordination. Which distribution is most expected?
options: Right upper-extremity ataxia with normal left-sided coordination
Bilateral complete paralysis below the neck
Left-sided appendicular ataxia
Contralateral loss of pain and temperature
Ipsilateral lower motor neuron facial paralysis exclusively
explanation: Cerebellar hemisphere lesions typically produce ipsilateral coordination deficits, including dysmetria and intention tremor.

stem: In the coronal section shown, a gray matter nucleus lies lateral to the globus pallidus and medial to the external capsule. Together with the caudate nucleus, it constitutes a major component of the striatum. Which structure is being identified?
options: Putamen
Subthalamic nucleus
Thalamus
Claustrum
Substantia nigra
explanation: The putamen is lateral to the globus pallidus and forms part of the striatum with the caudate.

stem: A patient has a mass at the cerebellopontine angle causing progressive unilateral sensorineural hearing loss, diminished vestibular function, and eventual ipsilateral facial weakness. In the ventral brainstem diagram, the affected cranial nerves emerge near the lateral pontomedullary junction. Which pair of nerves is most directly involved?
options: CN III and CN IV
CN V and CN VI
CN IX and CN X
CN VII and CN VIII
CN XI and CN XII
explanation: CN VII and VIII course through the cerebellopontine angle. Masses there may affect hearing, vestibular function, and facial movement.

stem: A patient develops hyperkalemia and nerve membranes initially become less negative because potassium's outward chemical gradient is reduced. Which localization, mechanism, or structure best explains the presentation?
options: Extracellular potassium elevation depolarizing resting membrane
TTX-sensitive voltage-gated sodium channel blockade
Sodium channel inactivation after sustained depolarization
Relative refractory period with persistent potassium conductance
Absolute refractory period from sodium inactivation
explanation: Key takeaway: Resting membrane voltage is dominated by K+ permeability, and increasing extracellular K+ depolarizes it A (Extracellular potassium elevation depolarizing resting membrane): This fits: Resting membrane voltage is dominated by K+ permeability, and increasing extracellular K+ depolarizes it B (TTX-sensitive voltage-gated sodium channel blockade): Not the best answer: Voltage-gated Na+ influx underlies rapid depolarization in typical axons C (Sodium channel inactivation after sustained depolarization): Not the best answer: Persistent depolarization favors the inactivated state of voltage-gated sodium channels D (Relative refractory period with persistent potassium conductance): Not the best answer: Elevated K+ conductance and incomplete Na+ recovery underlie relative refractoriness E (Absolute refractory period from sodium inactivation): Not the best answer: Na+ channels remain inactivated during the absolute refractory period

stem: A clinical team is distinguishing Sodium channel inactivation after sustained depolarization from related diagnoses, structures, and mechanisms in Action Potentials. Which observation is most consistent with the named finding?
options: Resting membrane potential moves toward a less-negative potassium equilibrium potential
Failure of the normal fast action-potential upstroke
Reduced available voltage-gated sodium channels and failed repetitive action potential initiation
Raised threshold for a second impulse during afterhyperpolarization
Faster propagation through increased membrane resistance and reduced capacitance
explanation: Key takeaway: Persistent depolarization favors the inactivated state of voltage-gated sodium channels A (Resting membrane potential moves toward a less-negative potassium equilibrium potential): Not the best answer: Resting membrane voltage is dominated by K+ permeability, and increasing extracellular K+ depolarizes it B (Failure of the normal fast action-potential upstroke): Not the best answer: Voltage-gated Na+ influx underlies rapid depolarization in typical axons C (Reduced available voltage-gated sodium channels and failed repetitive action potential initiation): This fits: Persistent depolarization favors the inactivated state of voltage-gated sodium channels D (Raised threshold for a second impulse during afterhyperpolarization): Not the best answer: Elevated K+ conductance and incomplete Na+ recovery underlie relative refractoriness E (Faster propagation through increased membrane resistance and reduced capacitance): Not the best answer: Myelin permits faster saltatory conduction by restricting transmembrane current loss

stem: A neuronal mutation slows voltage-gated potassium activation and lengthens the falling phase of the spike. Which localization, mechanism, or structure best explains the presentation?
options: Sodium channel inactivation after sustained depolarization
Delayed rectifier potassium channel opening
Relative refractory period with persistent potassium conductance
TTX-sensitive voltage-gated sodium channel blockade
Increased myelination reducing capacitance
explanation: Key takeaway: Voltage-gated K+ channels facilitate action-potential repolarization A (Sodium channel inactivation after sustained depolarization): Not the best answer: Persistent depolarization favors the inactivated state of voltage-gated sodium channels B (Delayed rectifier potassium channel opening): This fits: Voltage-gated K+ channels facilitate action-potential repolarization C (Relative refractory period with persistent potassium conductance): Not the best answer: Elevated K+ conductance and incomplete Na+ recovery underlie relative refractoriness D (TTX-sensitive voltage-gated sodium channel blockade): Not the best answer: Voltage-gated Na+ influx underlies rapid depolarization in typical axons E (Increased myelination reducing capacitance): Not the best answer: Myelin permits faster saltatory conduction by restricting transmembrane current loss

stem: A clinical team is distinguishing TTX-sensitive voltage-gated sodium channel blockade from related diagnoses, structures, and mechanisms in Action Potentials. Which observation is most consistent with the named finding?
options: Raised threshold for a second impulse during afterhyperpolarization
Failure of the normal fast action-potential upstroke
Reduced available voltage-gated sodium channels and failed repetitive action potential initiation
Complete immediate failure to initiate another spike after a prior action potential
Resting membrane potential moves toward a less-negative potassium equilibrium potential
explanation: Key takeaway: Voltage-gated Na+ influx underlies rapid depolarization in typical axons A (Raised threshold for a second impulse during afterhyperpolarization): Not the best answer: Elevated K+ conductance and incomplete Na+ recovery underlie relative refractoriness B (Failure of the normal fast action-potential upstroke): This fits: Voltage-gated Na+ influx underlies rapid depolarization in typical axons C (Reduced available voltage-gated sodium channels and failed repetitive action potential initiation): Not the best answer: Persistent depolarization favors the inactivated state of voltage-gated sodium channels D (Complete immediate failure to initiate another spike after a prior action potential): Not the best answer: Na+ channels remain inactivated during the absolute refractory period E (Resting membrane potential moves toward a less-negative potassium equilibrium potential): Not the best answer: Resting membrane voltage is dominated by K+ permeability, and increasing extracellular K+ depolarizes it

stem: Two suprathreshold pulses are delivered too close together and the second pulse cannot trigger a propagated spike regardless of stimulus intensity. Which localization, mechanism, or structure best explains the presentation?
options: Sodium channel inactivation after sustained depolarization
Absolute refractory period from sodium inactivation
TTX-sensitive voltage-gated sodium channel blockade
Delayed rectifier potassium channel opening
Relative refractory period with persistent potassium conductance
explanation: Key takeaway: Na+ channels remain inactivated during the absolute refractory period A (Sodium channel inactivation after sustained depolarization): Not the best answer: Persistent depolarization favors the inactivated state of voltage-gated sodium channels B (Absolute refractory period from sodium inactivation): This fits: Na+ channels remain inactivated during the absolute refractory period C (TTX-sensitive voltage-gated sodium channel blockade): Not the best answer: Voltage-gated Na+ influx underlies rapid depolarization in typical axons D (Delayed rectifier potassium channel opening): Not the best answer: Voltage-gated K+ channels facilitate action-potential repolarization E (Relative refractory period with persistent potassium conductance): Not the best answer: Elevated K+ conductance and incomplete Na+ recovery underlie relative refractoriness

stem: A clinical team is distinguishing Relative refractory period with persistent potassium conductance from related diagnoses, structures, and mechanisms in Action Potentials. Which observation is most consistent with the named finding?
options: Slower action-potential repolarization with prolonged depolarization
Complete immediate failure to initiate another spike after a prior action potential
Reduced available voltage-gated sodium channels and failed repetitive action potential initiation
Faster propagation through increased membrane resistance and reduced capacitance
Raised threshold for a second impulse during afterhyperpolarization
explanation: Key takeaway: Elevated K+ conductance and incomplete Na+ recovery underlie relative refractoriness A (Slower action-potential repolarization with prolonged depolarization): Not the best answer: Voltage-gated K+ channels facilitate action-potential repolarization B (Complete immediate failure to initiate another spike after a prior action potential): Not the best answer: Na+ channels remain inactivated during the absolute refractory period C (Reduced available voltage-gated sodium channels and failed repetitive action potential initiation): Not the best answer: Persistent depolarization favors the inactivated state of voltage-gated sodium channels D (Faster propagation through increased membrane resistance and reduced capacitance): Not the best answer: Myelin permits faster saltatory conduction by restricting transmembrane current loss E (Raised threshold for a second impulse during afterhyperpolarization): This fits: Elevated K+ conductance and incomplete Na+ recovery underlie relative refractoriness

stem: Two equal-diameter axons are compared; the more extensively myelinated axon conducts faster despite identical transmitter mechanisms. Which localization, mechanism, or structure best explains the presentation?
options: Increased myelination reducing capacitance
Sodium channel inactivation after sustained depolarization
TTX-sensitive voltage-gated sodium channel blockade
Relative refractory period with persistent potassium conductance
Absolute refractory period from sodium inactivation
explanation: Key takeaway: Myelin permits faster saltatory conduction by restricting transmembrane current loss A (Increased myelination reducing capacitance): This fits: Myelin permits faster saltatory conduction by restricting transmembrane current loss B (Sodium channel inactivation after sustained depolarization): Not the best answer: Persistent depolarization favors the inactivated state of voltage-gated sodium channels C (TTX-sensitive voltage-gated sodium channel blockade): Not the best answer: Voltage-gated Na+ influx underlies rapid depolarization in typical axons D (Relative refractory period with persistent potassium conductance): Not the best answer: Elevated K+ conductance and incomplete Na+ recovery underlie relative refractoriness E (Absolute refractory period from sodium inactivation): Not the best answer: Na+ channels remain inactivated during the absolute refractory period

stem: A second action potential occurs only with stronger stimulation shortly after the first because membrane excitability has not fully recovered. Which localization, mechanism, or structure best explains the presentation?
options: Relative refractory period with persistent potassium conductance
Absolute refractory period from sodium inactivation
Delayed rectifier potassium channel opening
Sodium channel inactivation after sustained depolarization
TTX-sensitive voltage-gated sodium channel blockade
explanation: Key takeaway: Elevated K+ conductance and incomplete Na+ recovery underlie relative refractoriness A (Relative refractory period with persistent potassium conductance): This fits: Elevated K+ conductance and incomplete Na+ recovery underlie relative refractoriness B (Absolute refractory period from sodium inactivation): Not the best answer: Na+ channels remain inactivated during the absolute refractory period C (Delayed rectifier potassium channel opening): Not the best answer: Voltage-gated K+ channels facilitate action-potential repolarization D (Sodium channel inactivation after sustained depolarization): Not the best answer: Persistent depolarization favors the inactivated state of voltage-gated sodium channels E (TTX-sensitive voltage-gated sodium channel blockade): Not the best answer: Voltage-gated Na+ influx underlies rapid depolarization in typical axons

stem: Local marine toxin exposure selectively prevents rapid depolarizing spikes without initially destroying passive membrane resistance. Which localization, mechanism, or structure best explains the presentation?
options: Absolute refractory period from sodium inactivation
Delayed rectifier potassium channel opening
Relative refractory period with persistent potassium conductance

Putamen in lateral lentiform nucleus
Vagus nerve postolivary rootlets
Facial and vestibulocochlear nerves at cerebellopontine angle
Cerebellar vermis lesion
explanation: Key takeaway: Globus pallidus includes internal and external output-related basal ganglia components A (Globus pallidus in medial lentiform nucleus): This fits: Globus pallidus includes internal and external output-related basal ganglia components B (Putamen in lateral lentiform nucleus): Not the best answer: Putamen is lateral lentiform nucleus and pairs with caudate as striatum C (Vagus nerve postolivary rootlets): Not the best answer: CN X exits from the postolivary region of lateral medulla D (Facial and vestibulocochlear nerves at cerebellopontine angle): Not the best answer: CN VII and VIII emerge together near lateral pontomedullary junction E (Cerebellar vermis lesion): Not the best answer: Cerebellar vermis coordinates axial and proximal postural control
